summary: Briefly describes how the Augmentation Research Center at SRI conceptualized and used graphics terminals. Everything described had been operational for months. Attention had centered on displaying text, with pictures next.

plainLanguage.summary: SRI's Augmentation Research Center describes its working text-display system. Programs could manage screen areas and text strings, and NLS could show several file views at once.

subtitle: How SRI-ARC organized text and file views on graphics displays.

tldr.problem: Programs needed a consistent way to control text displays across local and remote terminals.
tldr.mechanism: ARC treats each rectangular display area like a writable file and assigns identifiers to areas and strings so programs can manipulate them.
tldr.outcome: NLS users could switch between display and teletype modes and view or edit multiple files in separate display areas.

today: RFC 191 is a graphics implementation report published in July 1971. The unit metadata lists its status as Unknown.

sections.title: The Conceptual Display
sections.content:
ARC described graphics terminals as allocatable rectangular display areas. A program requests an area and its screen attributes, then receives an identifier for later changes. Each string written into an area also receives an identifier that can be used to move, delete, replace or restyle it.

The implemented text-display features included character size, horizontal spacing and font characteristics. Programs could also suppress individual strings or whole areas.
sections.plainLanguage: A program can request a rectangle on the screen and write text into it. Identifiers let the program later move, remove or change that text.

sections.title: Display and Teletype Modes
sections.content:
A terminal could switch between display mode and teletype simulation mode. In display mode, cursor coordinates arrived with each character and the teletype area was hidden. In teletype mode, user-owned display areas were hidden and cursor coordinates were not included with each character.

At TENEX startup, the system allocated a teletype simulation area and cursor for each local display terminal.
sections.plainLanguage: The terminal could show managed display areas or act like a typewriter terminal. Switching modes changed what appeared and what cursor information the program received.

sections.title: NLS and Multiple File Views
sections.content:
NLS formatters used a virtual display model with addressable points, different character sizes and fonts, and 7-bit ASCII. Post-processors adapted formatted output for a display, printer, microfilm device or teletype.

NLS also allowed a user to split a file-viewing area horizontally or vertically, so several files could be viewed and edited. The cursor's position helped determine which area a command affected.
sections.plainLanguage: NLS formatted content for different output devices. It could also divide the display so users could work with several files at once.
